nameStory: This tiny fungus doesn't have a widely-used common name, so we know it by its scientific name Paraeutypella decorticata. The species name 'decorticata' comes from Latin meaning 'stripped of bark' or 'peeled,' referring to how this fungus helps break down the outer layers of dead wood as it grows.
description: Paraeutypella decorticata is a microscopic wood-decaying fungus that forms tiny black dots on dead hardwood branches and twigs. These pinhead-sized structures, called perithecia, are the fungus's reproductive organs that poke through the bark surface like miniature volcanoes. The fungus itself lives invisibly within the dead wood, slowly breaking it down, while only these small black fruiting bodies reveal its presence. Each perithecium is roughly 1-2mm across—about the size of a peppercorn.

idTips.label: Black fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for clusters of tiny black dots scattered across dead bark, each about the size of a pinhead and slightly raised above the surface like small bumps

idTips.label: Hardwood host preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on dead branches of oak, maple, birch, and other hardwood trees—rarely seen on conifers like pine or spruce

idTips.label: Bark surface emergence
idTips.description: The black dots push through loose or peeling bark, sometimes causing small cracks or splits in the bark around each fruiting body

idTips.label: Branch size preference
idTips.description: Most commonly found on dead twigs and small branches 1-4 inches thick, rather than on large trunk surfaces or very thin twiglets

idTips.label: Clustered arrangement
idTips.description: Fruiting bodies appear in loose groups or lines along the branch, not randomly scattered—often following the grain of the wood beneath

habitat: Look for this fungus on dead hardwood branches in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England's lowlands and hills. It's particularly common on fallen oak and maple branches in mature woodlands, as well as dead limbs still attached to living trees. You'll find it from sea level up to mid-elevations, wherever hardwood debris accumulates on the forest floor or hangs in the canopy.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruiting bodies begin developing as temperatures warm, appearing as tiny dark bumps pushing through winter-softened bark.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when the black perithecia are most visible and mature, releasing spores during humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Fruiting bodies remain visible and active, especially after autumn rains provide moisture for continued spore release.
seasonality.winter: Old fruiting bodies persist as darkened spots on bark, though they become less active in cold weather and may be obscured by snow.

funFact: This fungus acts like nature's tiny drilling crew—each fruiting body can shoot spores up to several inches away through a microscopic cannon-like mechanism, helping colonize new dead wood with remarkable precision.
confusionNotes: The tiny black fruiting bodies can be mistaken for insect eggs or small scale insects on bark, but unlike biological spots, these fungal structures are firmly embedded in the bark and won't scrape off easily with a fingernail.
contextualKnowledge: Like many fungi in the Diatrypaceae family, this species plays a crucial ecological role as a primary decomposer, beginning the process of breaking down dead wood that other organisms will continue. The scientific naming system helps us track these ecologically important but often overlooked species.
compareHints: Paraeutypella decorticata differs from its relative P. vitis mainly in its host preference—while decorticata favors general hardwoods like oak and maple, P. vitis specifically targets grapevines and related woody vines. Both produce similar tiny black fruiting bodies, but decorticata's perithecia tend to be slightly smaller and more densely clustered on the bark surface.
